strengths: The paper addresses a practical problem: improving fine-grained visual perception without processing the entire image at high resolution. Distilling response-conditioned attention into a question-conditioned RoI predictor is a coherent approach that avoids autoregressive decoding during localization.

Results cover four model variants across two families and multiple document, OCR, and visual perception benchmarks. Improvements are substantial on several tasks: LLaVA-1.5-7B gains 12.4 points on DocVQA, 12.6 on TextVQA, and 17.2 on V-Star.

The component ablations provide useful evidence for selective label assignment, sink-token removal, and masked upscaling. Additional experiments examine backbone depth, predictor depth, training-set size, and smoothing.

The approach requires no bounding-box supervision and freezes the original backbone. The 10K-sample experiment supports data efficiency on TextVQA and V-Star, while reported throughput exceeds ViCrop on both LLaVA scales.
weaknesses: The comparative evaluation does not sufficiently establish competitiveness. Only S2 and ViCrop are evaluated, despite the paper discussing closely related learned RoI approaches and explicitly borrowing initialization and training choices from TwigVLM. No comparison isolates the benefit over a comparable trained predictor or tests the approach on a contemporary native high-resolution backbone.

The V-Star comparison is particularly difficult to interpret: Section 4.2 states that ViCrop's image-cropping strategy was not used, without explaining precisely what was removed or providing its original configuration alongside the modified version. Since cropping is central to the baseline, this leaves the large claimed advantage unresolved.

The central claim of more precise localization is supported mainly through downstream answer accuracy and selected visualizations. There is no quantitative comparison of raw attention, cleaned pseudo-labels, and learned predictions using localization metrics, despite using ground-truth boxes for Figure 3. Changes in crop extent and visual-token allocation could contribute to the gains.

Important implementation and efficiency details are missing. The manuscript does not specify the sink-norm threshold, inference threshold, Gaussian-filter parameters, or how the original mask is geometrically aligned with features extracted from the resized crop. Throughput lacks absolute measurements, batch and generation settings, token-count distributions, and stage-level timings; the stated 1.5× localization speedup is not backed by a timing breakdown. The supplied manuscript also has a blank code link.

The novelty is primarily a combination of established attention grounding, sink removal, confidence-based pseudo-label selection, and an initialized transformer branch. The paper needs clearer positioning and controlled comparisons to demonstrate what is technically distinctive about this combination beyond its useful implementation.

Appendix E does not establish the claimed superiority of the actual method. It assumes noise models that are not validated for attention maps and compares an ideal conditional expectation against raw attention using that same expectation as the target. This does not prove improved true-foreground localization for a finite-data predictor trained with selectively masked BCE, nor does it justify the sample-dependent bounding-box masking procedure.

Some claims exceed the reported evidence. The abstract associates 10K training samples with improvements exceeding 10 points on DocVQA, but the 10K ablation does not report DocVQA; the main results use 152K samples. Results have no repeated-run uncertainty, and the protocol does not explain how benchmark-informed thresholds and architecture choices were separated from final evaluation. These gaps weaken the claims of exceptional data efficiency and generalization.

strengths: The problem is practically relevant: improving fine-grained visual perception without processing every image region at high resolution. Distilling response-guided attention into a question-conditioned RoI predictor is a coherent approach.
Reported improvements are substantial across four models from two families. For LLaVA-1.5-7B, SD-RPN improves DocVQA from 21.5 to 33.9, TextVQA from 46.1 to 58.7, and V* from 50.3 to 67.5.

The ablations cover label assignment, sink-token removal, upscaling strategy, backbone depth, predictor depth, and training-set size. They provide useful evidence that selective pseudo-label supervision improves over direct attention regression.

The appendix provides training hyperparameters, model-specific layer choices, prompts, and training pseudocode. The reported two-hour training cost on four A6000 GPUs suggests a reasonably accessible adaptation procedure.
weaknesses: The comparisons do not convincingly establish competitiveness. Only S2 and ViCrop are evaluated as competing methods, and neither is evaluated on DeepSeek-VL. Closely related learned RoI approaches discussed in the paper lack quantitative comparison. Section 4.2 also states that ViCrop's image-cropping strategy was not used on V*, without adequately specifying the modification or showing the original configuration; this makes a central comparison difficult to interpret.

The efficiency evidence is incomplete. Relative throughput is reported without absolute latency, batching and generation settings, visual-token counts, memory costs, or a measured stage-by-stage breakdown. The claimed 1.5× speedup specifically for RoI prediction is not substantiated by separate timing results. Matched visual-token or compute budgets are needed to isolate localization quality from additional image processing.

Important inference details remain unspecified: the sink-norm threshold, Gaussian-filter parameters, binarization threshold, and how the original mask is remapped to the cropped image's feature grid. Handling empty masks and crop limits is also unclear. These choices directly affect both accuracy and throughput, weakening reproducibility despite the useful training specification.

The central claim of higher-quality localization is supported mainly through downstream answer scores and selected successful examples. There are no quantitative localization comparisons between raw attention, refined pseudo-labels, and learned predictions. Figure 3 reports only approximately 40% foreground precision for high-attention tokens, making direct evidence of improved pseudo-label and proposal quality particularly important.

The contribution primarily combines established attention-based grounding, sink-token removal, confidence-based pseudo-label filtering, and copied transformer layers. This can constitute a useful empirical contribution, but the paper needs stronger positioning and controlled comparisons to establish what advances beyond the closest prior methods.

The data-efficiency framing exceeds the demonstrated evidence. Main results use 152K samples, whereas the 10K experiment covers only four benchmarks and does not include DocVQA, despite the abstract and introduction associating 10K training with gains on that benchmark. No repeated sampling or seed variability is reported, although V* performance varies noticeably and non-monotonically with training-set size.

Appendix E does not establish the claimed superiority of the proposed method. It compares an ideal conditional expectation against raw attention using error relative to that same conditional expectation, under unverified noise assumptions. It does not analyze finite-sample learning, selective-label bias, bounding-box-based exclusion, or the actual masked BCE objective. Consequently, it offers intuition rather than a theoretical guarantee of better localization.

strengths: SD-RPN addresses a useful practical problem: learning question-conditioned regions from the model’s own attention without bounding-box annotations or full-backbone fine-tuning. Combining denoised pseudo-labels with a partial-backbone predictor is technically plausible and clearly motivated.

Results cover four model configurations across two families and diverse perception benchmarks. Gains are substantial: LLaVA-1.5-7B improves from 21.5 to 33.9 on DocVQA, 46.1 to 58.7 on TextVQA, and 50.3 to 67.5 on V-Star.

The component ablations provide meaningful evidence for selective label assignment, sink-token removal, and masked upscaling. Additional experiments examine backbone depth, predictor depth, training-set size, and response source.
The reported accuracy–throughput trade-off improves over ViCrop on the main OCR comparison. The 10K-sample experiment also demonstrates useful gains with limited additional training data.
weaknesses: Comparisons do not sufficiently establish competitiveness against closely related learned RoI methods. Only S2 and ViCrop are evaluated directly, neither is compared on DeepSeek-VL, and the relationship to the inherited partial-backbone design deserves sharper positioning. Section 4.2 also states that ViCrop’s cropping strategy was omitted on V-Star without adequately explaining the modification or validating its fairness.

The central claim of more precise localization lacks direct quantitative evaluation. There are no localization IoU, foreground precision/recall, or pseudo-label quality comparisons. Downstream improvements and selected visualizations cannot fully distinguish better localization from changes in crop geometry and visual-token allocation.

Important implementation and efficiency details are missing: the sink-norm threshold, inference threshold, Gaussian-filter settings, crop resolution, mask-coordinate transformation, and empty-mask handling. Throughput lacks absolute latency, batching and decoding settings, token counts, and stage-level measurements. The reported two-hour training cost does not clearly identify whether response generation and pseudo-label extraction are included.

The abstract and introduction emphasize training with 10K pairs, while the principal results use 152K. Table 4b supports 10K-sample gains on TextVQA and V-Star but does not establish the corresponding DocVQA claim. The data-efficiency claim should be distinguished more clearly from the full-data results.

Appendix E provides intuition rather than a guarantee for the proposed method. Comparing the population conditional expectation against raw attention using that expectation itself as the target is insufficient to establish improved true foreground localization. The noise assumptions are unverified, and the analysis does not address selective-label bias, finite-sample learning, or bounding-box-based exclusion.

No repeated-run uncertainty or threshold-sensitivity analysis is reported, despite empirical selection of several layers and thresholds. The validation protocol for these choices is unclear. These gaps, together with incomplete baseline comparisons, leave the paper slightly below the acceptance threshold despite its promising empirical gains.

strengths: The method addresses a meaningful practical problem: improving fine-grained visual perception without region annotations or full-backbone fine-tuning. Distilling response-guided attention into a query-conditioned predictor is a coherent approach.

Evaluation spans three model families and diverse OCR, document, and high-resolution benchmarks. Reported gains are substantial, including LLaVA-1.5-7B improvements of 12.7 points on DocVQA and TextVQA, with additional gains on the stronger Qwen2.5-VL models.

Extensive ablations examine label assignment, sink-token removal, backbone depth, predictor depth, training-set size, thresholds, and upscaling strategies. These provide useful evidence that the proposed components contribute beyond simply regressing raw attention.

The resolution-versus-throughput comparison in Appendix C.1 strengthens the practical motivation. The 10K-sample experiments also demonstrate promising data efficiency, and qualitative failure cases acknowledge localization and spatial-reasoning limitations.
weaknesses: The V-Star comparison is compromised by the statement that ViCrop's image-cropping strategy was disabled, without explaining precisely what was removed or why this is fair for a cropping-based baseline. Comparisons with DeepEyes and Thyme use published results without establishing matched inference budgets. These issues weaken the claimed advantage over competing methods.

Hyperparameter selection appears to use the reported evaluation benchmarks: Table 5 selects a new default using OCRBench, TextVQA, POPE, and V-Star scores, including test benchmarks. No separate tuning split is identified. This weakens claims of unseen-benchmark generalization; repeated runs or uncertainty estimates are also absent.

Efficiency accounting is insufficiently specified. Appendix C.2 counts only the additional RPN layers for its 20x prediction-speed claim, treating initial backbone features as already available. However, inserting crop tokens before the question changes its causal context, so the extent of reusable computation needs explanation. Absolute end-to-end latency, token counts, memory, and pseudo-label-generation cost would make the efficiency claims more assessable.

Important reproduction details are missing, including the sink-token norm threshold, Gaussian-filter parameters, inference binarization threshold, and precise mask alignment after cropping and resizing. The pseudocode and training settings help, but do not fully specify the inference pipeline.

The novelty is primarily a combination of established attention grounding, sink removal, selective pseudo-labeling, and an intermediate-layer prediction branch. The distinction from TwigVLM and related region-prediction approaches needs sharper explanation. Moreover, downstream accuracy alone does not establish that the pseudo-labels or predicted regions are more accurate; quantitative localization precision, recall, or IoU would directly test this central claim.

Several claims exceed the evidence. The headline 10K-sample claim includes DocVQA, but the 10K ablation does not report DocVQA and the main experiments use 152K samples. Appendix F assumes favorable noise models and compares an ideal conditional expectation against itself; it does not establish improved localization for the actual selectively labeled BCE-trained predictor.

strengths: The method addresses a practical problem: improving fine-grained visual perception without bounding-box supervision or full-model fine-tuning. Distilling response-conditioned attention into a question-conditioned region predictor is a useful contribution.

The evaluation spans three model families and multiple OCR, document, and high-resolution benchmarks. Reported improvements are substantial, including LLaVA-1.5-7B gains of 12.7 points on DocVQA and TextVQA, with additional gains on the stronger Qwen2.5-VL models.

The ablations meaningfully examine label assignment, sink-token removal, predictor depth, training-set size, and upscaling strategy. Table 4b supports useful data efficiency: 10K samples yield improvements exceeding 10 points on TextVQA and V-Star.
The appendix strengthens the empirical case with resolution-throughput curves, an external grounding baseline, implementation pseudocode, and informative failure examples.
weaknesses: The evaluation does not establish a clean separation between hyperparameter selection and final testing. Section 4.3 selects a new default using results on the reported evaluation benchmarks, including V-Star and OCRBench, without identifying an independent development set. This weakens the claimed generalization and the interpretation of the final scores.

The V-Star comparison against ViCrop is problematic: Section 4.2 explicitly states that its image-cropping strategy was disabled, without adequately explaining the modification or providing the intact method's result. Because cropping is central to this comparison, a standard implementation and matched computational budgets are needed.

Efficiency accounting remains incomplete. Appendix C.2 compares a 10.3 ms RPN prediction step against a full external grounding model and argues that only the added RPN layers incur extra cost. However, inserting crop tokens before the question changes subsequent causal hidden states. The paper should specify precisely which computations are reused, provide a complete latency breakdown, and report memory and token counts. Table 1 also shows substantial end-to-end throughput reductions to 0.40–0.62 times the baseline.

The claimed improvement in localization is assessed mainly through downstream answer accuracy and qualitative maps. Quantitative localization precision, recall, or IoU would directly test whether denoising produces better pseudo-labels and whether the student localizes better than its teacher. No repeated-run uncertainty is reported for the ablation gains.

Reproducibility and claim calibration need improvement. The sink-norm threshold, inference binarization threshold, and Gaussian-filter settings are unspecified. Most headline experiments use 152K samples; the 10K ablation does not report DocVQA, despite the abstract implying a greater-than-10-point gain there with that training size.

The conceptual advance is primarily a combination of existing attention localization, copied intermediate transformer blocks, and confidence-based pseudo-labeling; its distinction from the closest architectural work needs sharper treatment. Appendix F does not provide a guarantee for the actual method: it compares an ideal conditional expectation against noisy attention under unverified noise assumptions, without accounting for finite-sample learning, selective-label bias, or the spatial crop procedure.

strengths: The paper addresses a useful practical problem: improving fine-grained visual perception without full-model fine-tuning or explicit region annotations. Distilling response-guided attention into a question-conditioned RoI predictor is a coherent approach.

The evaluation spans three model families and multiple scales. Reported gains are substantial: LLaVA-1.5-7B improves from 21.5 to 34.2 on DocVQA and from 50.3 to 70.7 on V*. Improvements on Qwen2.5-VL provide evidence that the approach remains useful beyond older, low-resolution backbones.

The component ablations support the proposed design. In Table 3, selective label assignment improves the average score from 59.0 to 61.4, and sink-token removal increases it to 62.4. Backbone depth, predictor depth, training-set size, and upscaling strategies are also investigated.

The efficiency evaluation includes measured throughput and a resolution-scaling comparison on Qwen2.5-VL. The 10K-sample experiments demonstrate useful data efficiency, while qualitative failure cases acknowledge localization and spatial-reasoning limitations.
weaknesses: Comparison fairness is unresolved. Section 4.2 explicitly states that ViCrop's image-cropping strategy was disabled on V*, without adequately explaining what was disabled or why this preserves a representative baseline. Since cropping is central to the competing approach, the large V* advantage requires comparison against its standard configuration. DeepEyes and Thyme results also lack matched runtime and input-budget comparisons.

Hyperparameter selection appears to use evaluation benchmarks. Table 5 selects a stronger default using OCRBench, TextVQA, POPE, and V* results, and that configuration supplies the main reported LLaVA results. No separate tuning split is identified. This weakens the claimed generalization to unseen benchmarks, especially alongside architecture-specific empirical layer selection.

Efficiency accounting needs greater precision. Appendix C.2 compares a 10.3 ms RPN step with an external model's full prediction cost while treating backbone features as already available. The initial partial backbone pass, crop encoding, and recomputation after inserting visual tokens need an explicit cost breakdown and cache-reuse description. End-to-end throughput measurements are helpful, but do not establish the broader claim that the only additional cost is three predictor layers.

Important reproduction details are missing, including the sink-norm threshold, inference binarization threshold, Gaussian-filter settings, and precise mask alignment after cropping and re-encoding. Average added visual-token counts, inference batching, and whether the reported two-hour training cost includes pseudo-label generation are also unclear.

The architectural novelty is incremental relative to the cited work on middle-layer grounding, attention-sink removal, and TwigVLM-style branches. A sharper distinction from these methods and direct localization measurements would better establish that the contribution improves region prediction itself, beyond downstream benefits from additional visual input.

The abstract overstates the small-data evidence: Table 4b supports greater-than-10-point gains with 10K samples on TextVQA and V*, but does not report DocVQA, and the main experiments use 152K samples. No repeated runs or uncertainty estimates are provided despite nonmonotonic data-scaling results.

Appendix F does not establish the claimed superiority of the implemented method. Its conditional-expectation argument assumes noise models that are not validated for attention, measures error against the conditional expectation itself, and does not analyze selective labeling, ignored regions, or finite-sample learning. It should be framed as intuition rather than a guarantee.
